findings.failure_scenario: When `rank_invoice_entries` is called with a list of invoice entries, the first entry is silently ignored. The returned list will be missing the first entry, leading to incomplete or incorrect ranking results.
findings.suggestion:
for position in range(len(entries)):
    entry = entries[position]
findings.title: Off-by-one error in loop skips the first entry

findings.body: The function `register_shipment_events` uses a mutable default argument `events: list[str] = []`. This list is created once at function definition time and shared across all calls. Appending to it in one call will persist the state for subsequent calls.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `register_shipment_events("type_a")` then `register_shipment_events("type_b")` will result in the second call returning `{"type_b": ["type_a", "type_b"]}` instead of `{"type_b": ["type_b"]}`, causing unexpected accumulation of events across unrelated calls.
findings.title: Mutable default argument causes state leakage

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The function `register_shipment_events` uses a mutable default argument `events: list[str] = []`. In Python, default arguments are evaluated once at function definition time. This means all calls to the function without an explicit `events` argument will share the same list, causing events to accumulate across calls unexpectedly.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes `register_shipment_events('type_a')` and gets `{'type_a': ['type_a']}`. A subsequent caller invokes `register_shipment_events('type_b')` and gets `{'type_b': ['type_a', 'type_b']}` because the default list was mutated in the first call. This leads to data leakage and incorrect event tracking.
findings.title: Mutable default argument causes shared state across calls
